title: Traditional Crafts
description: Ten stories and columns about people who work with their hands: a shoemaker, a potter, a fisherman, a baker, a watchmaker, a quilter, a blacksmith, a printer, a teacher and a woodworker.

lessons.title: Boots for a Mail Carrier
lessons.summary: A shoemaker makes a pair of comfortable boots for a mail carrier whose old boots hurt.
lessons.text:
Samuel Ortiz has made shoes and boots in the same narrow shop for almost thirty years. He is a quiet man in his fifties, with gray hair and steady hands. The shop smells of leather, and its old wooden floor makes a soft sound under every step.

One cold morning in October, a woman named Elena came in. She was a mail carrier, and she walked about ten miles a day.

"Good morning," she said. "I need help. My boots are only a year old, but they have become painful. By the afternoon my feet hurt so much that I can hardly finish my route."

Samuel asked her to sit down and take off the boots. He held them up to the light from the window and turned them slowly. The soles were worn thin on the outside edge, and the toes were too narrow for her feet.

"These boots were made by a machine for an average foot," he said. "But nobody has an average foot. Your toes need more room, and your soles need to be thicker so that you do not feel every stone in the road."

"Can you make me a new pair?" Elena asked.

"I can, provided that you are patient," he said with a smile. "Good boots take time."

He measured both of her feet with a steady hand and wrote the numbers in a small book. Then he asked about her preferences. Elena said that her only real preference was comfort. She wore her boots at work, but she also wanted something casual enough to wear on weekends.

For three weeks, Samuel worked on the boots in the evenings. He cut the leather by hand and shaped it over a wooden model of her foot. He chose a thick rubber sole, because a leather sole would wear out too quickly on city streets. When he could not find the right brown thread, he used a dark red one as a substitute. In the end, he decided that the substitute looked even better, so he kept it.

When Elena came back, she put on the new boots and walked up and down the shop. Her toes had room to move, and the thick soles felt soft and strong at the same time.

"They aren't painful at all," she said. "They feel like casual shoes, but they look like real work boots."

Samuel smiled. For him, that was the best part of the job.

Questions:
How old is Samuel, and what are his hands like?
He is in his fifties, and he has steady hands.
Why had Elena's boots become painful?
They had become painful because the soles were worn thin and the toes were too narrow for her feet.
What was Elena's only real preference?
Her only real preference was comfort.
Why did Samuel choose a thick rubber sole?
He chose it because a leather sole would wear out too quickly on city streets.
What did Samuel use as a substitute for brown thread?
He used a dark red thread as a substitute.
How did the new boots feel?
They were not painful at all, and they felt like casual shoes.

lessons.title: Plates for a Chef
lessons.summary: A potter and a chef work together on a set of handmade plates for his new restaurant.
lessons.text:
My name is Iris, and my studio is a small room behind my house. I make bowls, cups and plates from clay on a wheel that turns under my hands.

Last spring, a chef named Marco Rossi knocked on my door. He was opening a small restaurant in town, and he wanted plates that nobody else had.

"I have been to every store in the city," he said. "Their plates are fine, but they all look the same. My food is simple, so the plates must have character."

He showed me his menu. It was short: fresh fish, vegetables from local farms, and bread from a shop down the street. The menu would change with the seasons, so the plates had to work with many dishes.

It was a substantial order: 40 large plates, 40 small ones and 20 bowls. For a studio like mine, that meant several months of work. I said yes at once, although I was nervous.

Our collaboration began the following week. I made 5 sample plates, each a little different. Some had wide edges, and others were almost flat. Some were white, and others were the soft green of river stones. Marco took them to his kitchen and served food on them for a week. Then he came back with his feedback.

His feedback was honest and clear. The flat plates were too flat, because sauce ran off the edge. "Chefs differ in many things," he said, "but we all want the food to be the most important thing on the table."

I listened, and I went back to the wheel. Each plate begins as a ball of clay that I press down with the palm of my hand. My palms know the clay better than my eyes do: they feel when the walls are too thick or the center is not even. By the end of the summer, my palms were rough, and my studio was full of plates.

Plates made by hand always differ a little from each other, and Marco liked that.

On the day before the restaurant opened, I drove the plates there in careful stacks, with paper between them. Together, Marco and I arranged the plates on the long shelves of his kitchen. When everything was arranged, he stood back and looked at the shelves for a long time.

"This was a real collaboration, Iris," he said. "Thank you."

Now, when I eat at his restaurant, I sometimes turn my plate over to see my mark on the bottom. It is a small thing, but it makes me proud.

Questions:
Who knocked on Iris's door last spring?
A chef named Marco Rossi knocked on her door.
Why was the order substantial?
It was substantial because it meant 40 large plates, 40 small plates and 20 bowls, or several months of work.
What was Marco's feedback about the flat plates?
He said they were too flat, because sauce ran off the edge.
How does Iris begin each plate?
She presses a ball of clay down with the palm of her hand.
How did Iris bring the plates to the restaurant?
She drove them there in careful stacks, with paper between them.
What did Marco and Iris do with the plates?
They arranged them on the long shelves of his kitchen.

lessons.title: Nets on the Cape
lessons.summary: An old fisherman repairs his nets in winter and helps a wounded bird.
lessons.text:
At the end of the cape, where the road stops and the rocks begin, there is a gray wooden shed. Every winter morning, Thomas Reed sits outside it and repairs his fishing nets. He is 70 years old, and he has fished from this cape for most of his life.

Winter on the cape is savage. The wind comes straight off the Atlantic, and the waves throw cold water high over the rocks. On the worst mornings, Thomas's fingers feel almost frozen, so he keeps a small fire burning in an old metal barrel next to him.

Repairing nets is slow work. A net that has been through a storm is full of holes, and each hole must be closed by hand. Thomas does not mind.

His son Daniel sometimes asks him whether the job has become a burden. "You could buy new nets, Dad," he says. "It would be easier."

"It would be easier," Thomas answers, "but they wouldn't be mine."

People who visit the cape in summer often think it must be a lonely place in winter. In a way, it is. However, Thomas is rarely lonely, because the cape is full of wildlife. Seals rest on the rocks below the shed. Birds circle over the water, and in the evening a fox sometimes appears at the edge of the road, then disappears into the dry grass.

One morning in January, he found a wounded bird caught in an old piece of net amongst the rocks. One of its wings was hurt, and it was too weak to fly. Thomas knew that a wounded bird can bite. Still, it took him only a moment to find the courage to help. He wrapped the bird in his coat, cut the net away with his knife, and drove it to a wildlife center in town.

The woman at the center said that the bird would need several weeks to get better. "It took courage to pick it up," she told him. "Many people would have left it there."

Three weeks later, she called him. The bird was strong again. Thomas drove back to the cape with the bird in a box and opened the box at the edge of the rocks. The bird stood still for a second, then spread its wings and flew out over the water. Thomas watched until the bird seemed to disappear amongst the waves and the gray winter light.

Then he went back to his shed, sat down beside the fire and picked up his net again.

Questions:
Where does Thomas repair his nets?
He repairs them outside a wooden shed at the end of the cape.
Why does Thomas keep a fire next to him?
He keeps a fire because the winter is savage and his fingers feel almost frozen.
What does Daniel ask his father?
He asks whether the job has become a burden.
Why is Thomas rarely lonely on the cape?
He is rarely lonely because the cape is full of wildlife.
What did Thomas find one morning in January?
He found a wounded bird caught in an old piece of net amongst the rocks.
Where did Thomas take the bird?
He took it to a wildlife center in town.

lessons.title: Bread Before Dawn
lessons.summary: A baker gets up in the middle of the night to bake bread and serve her customers.
lessons.text:
Long before midnight, the lights in Rosa Martin's apartment above her bread shop go out. Rosa goes to bed at 8 in the evening, so that she can get up at 2 in the morning. When her friends are still awake at midnight, she is already asleep.

By 3 in the morning, Rosa is standing in the warm kitchen behind the shop, with flour on her arms. She has made bread on this corner for 22 years, and her father made it here before her.

Rosa cares about grain the way some people care about wine. She buys her flour from a family farm 2 hours away, where she can walk through the fields and see the grain growing. "Good bread begins in a field," she likes to say, "not in a kitchen."

The work in the dark hours follows a steady order. She mixes the dough, lets it rest, shapes it and lets it rest again. Unless the dough has enough time, the bread will be heavy, so she is never in a hurry.

Dawn comes slowly to the shop. First the window turns from black to dark blue, then to gray, and finally to soft gold. Just before dawn, the first breads are ready, and the whole street begins to smell of them.

At 6, Rosa opens the door. Her most frequent customer is Mr. Hayes, a bus driver who has started his day here every morning for 15 years. She greets him by name, and he greets her with the same comment about the weather every morning. Other frequent customers follow: nurses on their way home from the night shift and students on their way to class.

At 11, Rosa begins to make sandwiches for the lunch crowd. The most popular one is beef on dark bread. She cooks the beef herself the evening before.

Rosa knows that many of her customers count every penny, so she keeps her prices low. "I would rather sell 100 sandwiches at a fair price than 50 at a high one," she says. "For some people, every penny matters."

At 2 in the afternoon, she says goodbye to her last customer. "Goodbye, see you tomorrow," she calls, and she locks the door. Then she sleeps for a few hours. People often ask her whether so little sleep is sufficient. She always gives the same answer: it is sufficient, provided that she loves her work. And she does.

Questions:
Why does Rosa go to bed at 8 in the evening?
She goes to bed early so that she can get up at 2 in the morning.
Where does Rosa buy her flour?
She buys it from a family farm 2 hours away, where she can see the grain growing.
How does the window of the shop change at dawn?
It turns from black to dark blue, then to gray, and finally to soft gold.
Who is Rosa's most frequent customer?
Her most frequent customer is Mr. Hayes, a bus driver.
What is the most popular sandwich?
The most popular sandwich is beef on dark bread.
Why does Rosa keep her prices low?
She keeps them low because many of her customers count every penny.

lessons.title: My Grandfather's Watch
lessons.summary: A young man takes his grandfather's broken watch to an old watchmaker.
lessons.text:
When my grandfather died last year, he left me his watch. It is a simple silver watch, and he wore it every day for more than 60 years. It is not worth much money. Still, to me it is precious, a real treasure, because I remember it on his arm when he taught me to fish.

Two months ago, the watch stopped. I tried everything, but the hands did not move. I was desperate. I took it to a jewelry store at the mall, where a young man looked at it for ten seconds. "It's unlikely that anyone can fix this," he said. "They don't make parts for these anymore."

A week later, a friend told me about a watchmaker named Abel Stern. His shop is on Ash Street, between a hardware store and a laundry.

Inside, dozens of clocks were ticking on the walls. Mr. Stern was a small man with white hair, sitting at a heavy stone table. He told me that the table was made of stone for the sake of stability. "When you work with parts this small," he said, "stability is everything. If the table shakes, the part flies away."

He opened the back of the watch and looked inside through a small lens that he held in one eye. Through the lens, he said, a tiny screw looks as big as a coin. The problem was apparent to him at once: a small spring had broken. It was also apparent that he enjoyed the challenge. His face became calm and intent, like the face of a person reading a good book.

"The watch must undergo a full cleaning as well as the repair," he said. "It will take three weeks."

"Is it unlikely that you will find the part?" I asked.

"Unlikely, yes. Impossible, no," he said. "I have drawers full of old parts. And if I don't have the right one, I can make it."

For three weeks, Mr. Stern was intent on the job. Once he called to say that he had found a spring and shaped it so that it fit perfectly.

When I returned, the watch was ticking on a soft cloth on his table. It looked exactly the same, but it sounded alive again. I asked him why he still did such slow work at his age.

"Time is precious," he said. "So are the things that measure it."

Now I wear the watch every day, just as my grandfather did.

Questions:
Why is the watch a treasure to the writer?
It is a treasure because it belonged to his grandfather, who wore it every day for more than 60 years.
Why was the writer desperate?
He was desperate because the watch had stopped and he could not make it work.
What did the young man at the jewelry store say?
He said it was unlikely that anyone could fix the watch.
Where is Mr. Stern's shop?
It is on Ash Street, between a hardware store and a laundry.
Why is Mr. Stern's table made of stone?
It is made of stone for the sake of stability.
What was the problem with the watch?
A small spring had broken.
What did the watch have to undergo besides the repair?
It had to undergo a full cleaning.

lessons.title: The Bunny Quilt
lessons.summary: An old quilter in the mountains of Kentucky teaches a young neighbor to make a quilt.
lessons.text:
In a small town in the mountains of eastern Kentucky, Opal Harmon has made quilts for almost 70 years. A quilt is a warm bed cover made of many small pieces of cotton, joined together in a pattern. Opal learned from her mother, who cut the squares from old shirts and dresses. Over the years, Opal has made more than 200 quilts and distributed most of them to friends and new babies.

Opal's house sits on a hill. From the summit, on a clear day, you can see three valleys and the blue line of the mountains beyond them.

Last fall, a girl from the next house, Lily, asked if Opal would teach her. Lily was 14 and had never held a needle. Opal was happy to give her guidance. Every Saturday afternoon, they sat together at the kitchen table. Opal's guidance was simple: small, even lines of thread and no hurry.

Lily wanted to make a quilt for her baby cousin. She chose a pattern of white bunnies on squares of light blue and yellow. Cutting out the bunnies was hard, and joining them was harder. More than once, Lily cursed under her breath when the needle went into her finger. Opal pretended not to hear. "My mother cursed too," she said. "Every quilt has a little of that in it."

While they worked, Opal told Lily about the gatherings of her youth. In those days, women from the whole valley met in one house to finish a quilt together. Those gatherings were full of talk and food.

She also explained that, for a long time, museums did not show this work as art. Opal called it a quiet kind of discrimination against women's work. Today that has changed. Work from these mountains now hangs in prominent museums, and people write long books about it. Opal enjoys those books, although she laughs at some of the interpretations. "One man wrote that the dark colors in my mother's work were about loss," she said. "That's one interpretation. The real reason is that she only had brown cotton that year."

On Christmas Eve, the bunny quilt was finished. Lily's family held a small gathering at their house, and the gifts were distributed after dinner. When the baby's mother opened the quilt, she held it up so that everyone could see the bunnies. Then she gave it a prominent place, over the side of the baby's bed.

Opal sat near the fire and smiled, the way a teacher smiles when a lesson has worked.

Questions:
What is a quilt?
A quilt is a warm bed cover made of many small pieces of cotton, joined together in a pattern.
What can you see from the summit of the hill?
On a clear day, you can see three valleys and the mountains beyond them.
What was Opal's guidance?
Her guidance was simple: small, even lines of thread and no hurry.
What pattern did Lily choose?
She chose a pattern of white bunnies on light blue and yellow squares.
Why did Opal speak of a quiet kind of discrimination?
She spoke of it because, for a long time, museums did not show this work as art.
When was the bunny quilt finished?
It was finished on Christmas Eve.

lessons.title: The Blacksmith at the Fair
lessons.summary: A blacksmith shows his old craft at a county fair and is nominated for an award.
lessons.text:
Every August, the Hamilton County Fair fills a large field outside town with rides, music and the smell of fried food. Yet for many visitors, the main attraction is a small open shed at the far end of the field, where a blacksmith named Hank Weaver works.

Hank is a broad man with a gray beard and a leather coat covered in small burn marks. Around him lies his arsenal: hammers of every size, long iron tongs, a heavy iron block for shaping metal, and a fire of glowing coals. He has collected this arsenal over 40 years, and he knows every tool as well as his own hands.

He pushes a bar of iron into the fire and waits. When the iron glows bright orange, he pulls it out with the tongs and lays it on the block. Then the hammer comes down. Each time it slams into the hot metal, a burst of sparks flies into the air, and the children in the front row step back and laugh. The hammer slams down again and again, steady as a clock, and slowly the straight bar becomes a hook, a leaf or a small heart.

People arrive from all over the fair, attracted by the noise, and stay longer than they planned. This year the shed attracted more visitors than ever, for a simple reason. In July, a reporter from the local TV station had filmed Hank at work. Her footage was shown on the evening news and shared thousands of times online. The footage was only two minutes long, but it made Hank famous in the county.

Hank is pleased by the attention, but he has a more practical goal. He wants to recruit young people. "Most blacksmiths I know are older than me," he says. "If we don't recruit new people, this craft will disappear in 20 years." Between shows, he lets teenagers strike the hot iron under his guidance. Most give up after a few minutes, but one or two always come back the next day.

On the last evening, the fair gave an award to a person who keeps an old skill alive. Three people had been nominated: a woman who makes baskets, a man who trains horses, and Hank. When Hank's name was read, the crowd burst into loud cheers. He walked to the stage, still with black marks on his hands.

"I'm glad you nominated me," he said. "But I'd be even happier if one of those kids from my shed won this prize in 30 years."

Questions:
What is the main attraction of the fair for many visitors?
For many visitors, the main attraction is the shed where Hank works as a blacksmith.
What is in Hank's arsenal?
It has hammers, iron tongs, a heavy iron block and a fire.
What happens each time the hammer slams into the hot metal?
A burst of sparks flies into the air.
Why did the shed attract more visitors this year?
It attracted more visitors because a reporter's footage of Hank was shown on the news and shared online.
Why does Hank want to recruit young people?
He wants to recruit them because otherwise the craft will disappear in 20 years.

lessons.title: Ink on My Hands
lessons.summary: A printer who works on a hundred-year-old press writes about her craft.
lessons.text:
Ink on My Hands
By Clara Novak

In a world of laptops and phones, I spend my days with a machine that weighs as much as a small car. It is a printing press built in 1912, and it stands in a brick building on Water Street that used to be a garage. I print wedding invitations, posters, business cards and, once a year, a small literary magazine.

On a press like mine, each letter is a small block of metal. I set the letters by hand, one by one, in a frame, and lock the frame into the press. The press rolls ink over the letters and pushes them into thick, soft paper. The letters sit slightly deep in the paper, so that you can feel them with your fingers.

Visitors often ask me about handmade versus digital, as if one side must win. I don't see it as press versus laptop. I design many cards on my laptop before I set a single letter. The difference is in what you hold at the end.

My favorite job of the year is the literary magazine. A group of local writers send their poems and short stories to a retired English teacher named Mr. Grant, who has edited the magazine since it began. Once the pages are edited, I print 300 copies, one page at a time. This year's issue was edited with special care, because the magazine is now 20 years old. The writers had planned to celebrate at the spring book fair, but the fair was canceled because the heating in the hall was broken. So they held their party in my shop instead, amongst stacks of fresh paper.

Last spring, the high school asked me to help with a class on constitutional history. The students came to my shop to learn how documents were printed 200 years ago. I showed them that the first copies of our state constitution, and the reports of every legislative session that followed, were printed on presses much like mine. In those days, every legislative report and every newspaper headline was set by hand, letter by letter. One boy spent half an hour setting a headline of just four words, and he was proud of every letter.

On my phone, the email app is a tiny icon of an envelope. My press is the opposite of that icon: large, slow and impossible to delete. Some designers call the old press an icon of patient work. I simply call it my colleague.

Questions:
What does Clara print?
She prints wedding invitations, posters, business cards and a small literary magazine.
Who has edited the literary magazine since it began?
Mr. Grant, a retired English teacher, has edited it since it began.
Why was the spring book fair canceled?
It was canceled because the heating in the hall was broken.
What did the students learn in the class on constitutional history?
They learned how documents, such as the state constitution and the reports of legislative sessions, were printed 200 years ago.
How long did one boy spend setting a headline?
He spent half an hour setting a headline of just four words.

lessons.title: Keep the School Workshop Open
lessons.summary: A teacher explains why his high school should keep its wood workshop.
lessons.text:
Keep the School Workshop Open
By Peter Lund, teacher at Ridgeview High School

There is an ongoing debate in our school district about the wood workshop at Ridgeview High. Next year's budget is tight, and some members of the school board want to close the workshop and use the room for a new computer lab. The controversy has filled several meetings. I have taught in the workshop for 18 years, so you can guess which side I am on. Still, this controversy deserves a calm discussion.

The main argument for closing the workshop rests on an assumption: that the jobs of the future will all happen on screens. I understand this assumption, but I believe it is wrong. Our town still needs people who build and repair things, and many of them will retire soon. Someone will have to do this work, and nobody can learn to fix a roof in a virtual lesson.

I do not criticize computers. My students use them every day, and so do I. In fact, many of my students design their projects on a screen before they touch a piece of wood. What I criticize is the idea that the virtual world can replace the real one. A virtual table cannot hold your dinner.

There is another reason. Many young people today are dependent on their phones for almost everything: for directions, for answers and for fun. In the workshop, there is nothing to plug in except the machines. For 50 minutes, the students are dependent only on their own hands, their patience and each other. I have watched quiet students become confident when they finish their first chair. I have watched loud students become careful when they hold a sharp tool.

Some parents ask whether the workshop is safe. It is, provided that the rules are followed. Every student learns how to plug in, use and turn off each machine before working with it. In 18 years, we have had no serious injuries.

I have a proposal. Instead of closing the workshop, the school could give every student one slot a week in it during their first year. A single slot of 50 minutes is not much. Yet it might be enough to show some students a path they had never considered.

The board will vote in May. Whatever it decides, I hope the discussion stays friendly, because both sides want the same thing: a good future for our children.

Questions:
What is the ongoing debate in the school district about?
It is about whether to close the wood workshop and use the room for a computer lab.
What assumption does the argument for closing the workshop rest on?
It rests on the assumption that the jobs of the future will all happen on screens.
What does Mr. Lund criticize?
He criticizes the idea that the virtual world can replace the real one.
What are many young people dependent on?
They are dependent on their phones for almost everything.
What does every student learn before working with a machine?
Every student learns how to plug in, use and turn off each machine.
What does Mr. Lund suggest?
He suggests that every student get one slot a week in the workshop during their first year.

lessons.title: The Wooden Wall
lessons.summary: A woodworker makes a large wooden wall and a portrait for an old jazz club.
lessons.text:
The Blue Room is a small jazz club in New Orleans. It is an underground club in the simplest sense: to reach it, you go down a narrow set of steps from the street into a long room with brick walls. On most nights, the room is full of jazz until 2 in the morning.

Last year, the owner, Mrs. Della Price, decided that the long brick wall behind the stage needed something. So she called Leon Baptiste, who makes things from wood in a workshop two streets away.

Leon has made tables, doors and signs for 30 years, but he had never made anything so large. Mrs. Price wanted an installation: 12 tall wooden panels that would cover the whole wall, with musicians and instruments cut into the wood. She also asked for one more thing. On top of the old piano by the stage, she wanted a wooden bust of her father, who had opened the club in 1962 and played jazz there for 40 years.

For eight months, Leon's hands were occupied with almost nothing else. For each panel, he drew the design first and then began to cut. Leon explains that you must never be aggressive with wood. If you are too aggressive, you take away too much, and wood never grows back. So he worked slowly, following the grain and removing a little at a time.

The bust was the hardest part. Leon had only three old photos of Mr. Price, and none of them showed his face from the side. Leon worked on the bust in the evenings, when the workshop was quiet, and Mrs. Price visited every Sunday to give her opinion.

The installation itself was almost a nightmare. The panels were too tall to carry down the narrow steps, so Leon had to bring them in through a small door at the back of the building, one at a time. It took four people a whole day. "Those steps were my nightmare for a month," Leon said later. But every panel arrived without a mark.

When the installation was finished, the club held a special night. A band played the old songs that Mr. Price had loved. The wooden musicians on the wall seemed to move in the warm light, and on the piano the wooden bust looked out over the room with a calm, patient smile.

"He looks happy," Mrs. Price told Leon. "He always looked like that when the music was good."

Questions:
Why is the Blue Room called an underground club?
It is called underground because you reach it by going down a narrow set of steps from the street.
What did Mrs. Price want for the wall behind the stage?
She wanted an installation of 12 tall wooden panels.
Why must Leon not be aggressive with the wood?
If he is too aggressive, he takes away too much, and wood never grows back.
Why was the installation almost a nightmare?
It was almost a nightmare because the panels were too tall to carry down the narrow steps.
What were Leon's hands occupied with for eight months?
They were occupied with the panels and the bust.
